headline: Fans want the city's real second-line color on the jersey, not the tourist version
summary: The Pelicans launched in 2013 in navy, gold and red, and the Hornets' teal and purple stayed in Charlotte. With no classic era to mine, fans find their identity in New Orleans-made merch. The 2023-24 "NOLA Nights" City Edition was loved enough to return in 2025-26. The opening is local stories, built with the people who own those traditions.

insights.title: Young identity, no classic vault
insights.detail: The Pelicans brand dates to 2013, and the 2002-13 Hornets history sits with Charlotte. There is no multi-decade throwback vault to mine. Fans' emotional anchors are Anthony Davis, Chris Paul-era Hornets memories and Zion.
insights.implication: Classic Edition is a weak lever here. Put design energy into City Edition and lifestyle product built from the city, not the franchise archive.

insights.title: A returning City Edition shows what fans want
insights.detail: The 2025-26 City Edition reissued the 2023-24 design, which fans had singled out as a favorite. A team repeating a City Edition is a sign of unusually strong demand for one look.
insights.implication: Study what made the 2023-24 design land before briefing a 2026-27 concept, and don't swap it for something more generic. Verify the 2026-27 City Edition status first.

insights.title: Carnival colors are expected, and flat
insights.detail: Purple, green and gold is the city's default shorthand. The 2023-24 "Skelican" edition used purple and neon green, but as a night-life look. Locals take Carnival color for granted. They respond to specifics: krewe culture, the Zulu and Rex traditions, and the neighborhood second-line clubs.
insights.implication: Skip the generic three-color stripe. Use named, credited local references, with purple, green and gold in restraint against navy.

insights.title: Real merch lives outside the team shop
insights.detail: Local screen-printed shirts, Who Dat-style vernacular, Saints and Pelicans crossovers and neighborhood-pride tees (Seventh Ward, Ninth Ward, Westbank, Uptown) outsell generic team gear. Fans trade on area codes, wards and slang.
insights.implication: Work with local New Orleans printers and designers. Build neighborhood-first graphics that the team's own shop doesn't.

insights.title: The biggest untouched design language
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian suits, hand-sewn beadwork and feather work, and brass-band second-line parades from the Tremé and Seventh Ward are the city's most distinctive visual tradition. They are sacred and living, not decoration.
insights.implication: Treat it as a partnership, and credit and pay the tribes' and artists' communities. Borrow the logic (color layering, patchwork, hand-stitched texture), not the suit imagery.

insights.title: Zion and Murphy lead a rebuilding team
insights.detail: After two sub-30-win seasons, a 26-56 record and a coaching change to Jamahl Mosley, fan sentiment is cautious. Zion Williamson is still the marquee jersey. Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears are the younger faces.
insights.implication: Back player product (Zion, Murphy) and city pride, not team-performance stories. Keep launch volume measured.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: The Pelicans' home arena, next to the Superdome, where the city's pro-sports merch culture meets Who Dat Saints culture.

places.name: Louis Armstrong Park and Congo Square
places.why: The historic gathering site of African and Afro-Caribbean music and dance, and the cultural root of second-line and Black New Orleans music.

places.name: Backstreet Cultural Museum
places.why: A long-running museum of Mardi Gras Indian suits, social aid and pleasure club regalia and jazz funeral tradition. A respected partner for any cultural work.

places.name: Magazine Street
places.why: The boutique and streetwear spine, where New Orleans-made brands sell.

places.name: Dooky Chase's Restaurant
places.why: A landmark of Creole cooking and Black civil rights history, and the kind of heritage fans treat as the city's own.

places.name: Xavier University of Louisiana
places.why: A historically Black university with a strong local sports and style culture, and a youth-facing partner.

people.name: Zion Williamson
people.why: The franchise's biggest jersey draw and the most visible face of the team.

people.name: Trey Murphy III
people.why: A breakout scorer at 21.5 points per game last season, and a rising second face for product.

people.name: Derik Queen
people.why: A young big man acquired in the trade that cost the team its 2026 first-round pick.

people.name: Jeremiah Fears
people.why: A young guard in the team's new core.

people.name: Jamahl Mosley
people.why: The new head coach in 2026-27, replacing Willie Green.

people.name: Anthony Davis
people.why: The Pelicans-era icon whose number and unibrow-era jerseys fans still wear.

people.name: Trombone Shorty
people.why: A Tremé-born brass musician and ambassador for New Orleans music, with widely recognized imagery.

people.name: Big Freedia
people.why: The best-known face of bounce, a distinct local sound for neighborhood-first collaborations.

moments.name: Carnival season and Mardi Gras
moments.why: The city's biggest color moment, and the obvious, easy window for purple, green and gold product.

moments.name: Super Sunday and St. Joseph's Night
moments.why: The Mardi Gras Indian tribes' public gatherings. Offer respectful, credited partnership here, not product drops.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival
moments.why: The city's major music festival, and a spring moment for local culture far from the NBA.

moments.name: Southern Decadence and Essence Festival
moments.why: Essence Festival of Culture draws a large Black audience to the Superdome and Smoothie King Center area.

moments.name: NBA Cup group play
moments.why: The Pelicans are in West Group B with OKC, MIN, LAC and MEM, opening Cup play at the Clippers on Oct 30.

moments.name: Season opener
moments.why: The 2026-27 home opener is the first chance to show a new uniform set and the Mosley era.

moments.name: Saints season
moments.why: Football dominates local sports attention in the fall, so crossover product competes for the same fans.

designCues.cue: Pelicans navy as the base, with Carnival gold used as a thin accent
designCues.use: Keep navy dominant so the team stays recognizable. Use Carnival colors as accents, not full-body purple.

designCues.cue: Old gold, a muted gold that reads as brass rather than yellow
designCues.source: Official Pelicans gold, echoing brass instruments and wrought iron
designCues.use: Use for trim, numerals and metal-look hardware.

designCues.cue: Carnival purple as a restrained secondary
designCues.source: Mardi Gras color tradition (purple for justice)
designCues.use: Apply as a gradient or lining color. Avoid a full striped Carnival set.

designCues.cue: Wrought-iron balcony lacework as a line pattern
designCues.source: French Quarter and Garden District ironwork
designCues.use: Run it tone-on-tone on warm-ups and hoodies, drawn as a custom pattern, not a photo.

designCues.source: Second-line club regalia and social aid and pleasure club style
designCues.use: Reference layered fabric and trim in a collaboration with a local designer. Never copy specific club or tribe designs.

designCues.source: Corner stores, po-boy shops and neighborhood signs
designCues.use: Make a custom neighborhood-name wordmark for tees and hats, drawn by a New Orleans lettering artist.

designCues.cue: Fleur-de-lis reduced to a clean modern mark
designCues.source: City and state heraldry, already part of the Pelicans logo
designCues.use: Use sparingly, since the Saints and the city also own this symbol, and skip the stock clip-art version.

designCues.source: Local neighborhood identity, including the 504 area code
designCues.use: Build neighborhood tees with local artists, and credit them.

productHooks: Neighborhood capsule (Seventh Ward, Tremé, Central City, Ninth Ward, Westbank) designed with New Orleans artists, sold at Magazine Street shops and online.
Zion and Trey Murphy III player pack with ironwork-pattern graphics, in navy and old gold.
Carnival-season warm-up and shooting shirt with purple only as a lining, released ahead of Mardi Gras.
Bounce and brass-band capsule with a local artist, with royalties to the artist and a music-education partner.
Hat and jacket line with hand-painted shop-sign lettering for neighborhood names.
watchouts: Mardi Gras Indian suits, Black Masking Indian imagery and feather or bead designs are sacred, community-owned work. Don't copy them. If you engage at all, partner, credit and pay.
Who Dat and fleur-de-lis marks carry Saints and city licensing history. Check IP before using them.
Avoid tourist shorthand (Bourbon Street, voodoo, "Nawlins") and hurricane-trauma imagery.
Don't reference or imitate specific krewes' or second-line clubs' regalia without their consent.
Don't rely on the past City Edition detail in this file without checking. Concepts and years are from memory.

eras.look: Navy, gold and red, with a pelican-and-fleur-de-lis primary logo and a custom wordmark.
eras.legacy: The franchise's only identity as the Pelicans, tied to Anthony Davis and Zion Williamson.

eras.look: Teal, purple and gold, with the Hugo hornet mark.
eras.legacy: Fondly remembered in the city. The team history now sits with Charlotte, so New Orleans fans can't wear it as an official throwback.

cityEditions.concept: A reissue of the 2023-24 "NOLA Nights" / "Skelican" City Edition design.
cityEditions.note: The return signals strong demand for the 2023-24 look. Verify the 2026-27 City Edition.

cityEditions.concept: "NOLA Nights": vivid purple with neon green accents, skeletonized logos and a custom NOLA wordmark, inspired by the city's streets and lights at night.
cityEditions.note: A fan favorite, as its 2025-26 return shows.

cityEditions.concept: Concepts for the other seasons (2017-18 to 2022-23, 2024-25) were not verified. The 2024-25 edition exists, but its design wasn't checked.
cityEditions.note: Each season's concept and reception needs a live check.

untoldStories.story: The Seventh Ward and Tremé social aid and pleasure club second-line tradition, told with the clubs' permission.
untoldStories.why: It's the city's own parade culture, not a tourist symbol, and a jersey story should come from the community.

untoldStories.story: Congo Square and the roots of New Orleans music, from brass bands to bounce.
untoldStories.why: It ties the city's identity to a place and goes deeper than Mardi Gras color alone.

untoldStories.story: The levee-and-Gulf identity of the Ninth Ward and the West Bank, including post-Katrina rebuilding told by residents.
untoldStories.why: It gives neighborhoods outside the French Quarter a place on the product, if handled with care and local voices.

untoldStories.story: The Hornets-to-Pelicans transition and the 2005 return after Hurricane Katrina.
untoldStories.why: A lived franchise chapter that few fans see in product. It needs sensitivity.
